audience: A curious viewer with no background in timekeeping.
title: Every leap second on record has only ever been added, never undone.
question: Has a leap second ever been taken away?
alternates: Every leap second so far has been added
premise: Since 1972 civil time has been kept in step with the Earth's rotation by leap seconds. The IERS table lists every one; it answers whether any was ever subtracted.
whyWatch: Clocks can in principle lose a second as well as gain one. The record says which has actually happened.
tension: A negative leap second is allowed by the rules and talked about every few years; the question is whether one has ever been used.

arc.hook: A clock can be told to skip a second or to repeat one. Which has happened?
arc.conflict: The claims pulling in different directions: "Leap seconds exist because the Earth's rotation does not keep exact atomic time, so civil time is adjusted to stay within a second of it"; "Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away".
arc.evidence: The IERS table of TAI-UTC: 28 values from 10 s in 1972 to 37 s in 2017, each one second more than the last.
arc.resolution: Every leap second so far was added; none was ever taken away.
arc.takeaway: The next change, whichever direction, will be announced in Bulletin C.

evidence.note: The IERS table of TAI-UTC lists 28 values from 10 s on 1 January 1972 to 37 s on 1 January 2017, each exactly one second larger than the one before: every one of the 27 steps added a second and none subtracted one.
evidence.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded
